summary: A proposal from UCSB to study how well newcomers can use the ARPANET. A group of 14 graduate students would try the computers at server sites and answer questions about user problems, site limits, where to edit files, and running cooperating processes at several sites.

eli5.summary: A class of students will try the network as beginners and report what is confusing, so it can be improved.

how hard was it to use the arpanet in 1972
subtitle: UCSB plans a classroom test of how well newcomers can learn to use ARPANET server sites.

tldr.problem: No one knew whether a technically competent but uninformed person could learn to solve problems at ARPANET server sites, or what would get in the way.
tldr.mechanism: A test group of 14 graduate students at UCSB, using a 16-console classroom tied to the UCSB 360-75 host, would try the network sites and report what they found.
tldr.outcome: The RFC lists five questions and nine early comments, and promises periodic follow-up reports. Its status is listed as Unknown.

today: The RFC's status is listed as Unknown, and no RFC replaces or updates it according to the metadata. It is an early-1972 proposal and progress report for a usability study, and it contains no final results.

sections.title: The Questions
sections.content:
The RFC poses five questions. Can a technically competent person, new to the network and to its different time-shared terminal systems, become good at solving problems at server sites? What user problems make that hard? Once skilled, what limits usability, and what should change at server and user sites?

The last two ask whether a user should compose and edit all files at one site for transfer elsewhere, or learn the editors at each site, and what problems arise in starting cooperating processes at several sites and controlling them.
sections.eli5: The big question is whether a smart beginner can learn the network alone, and what trips them up.

sections.title: How the Test Is Run
sections.content:
Under UCSB Professor James Howard, a test group of 14 graduate students was formed. They use the 16-console On-Line System classroom in the E.E. Department at UCSB, which is tied into the UCSB Host 360-75 and so reaches the network. The consoles are old-style Culler-Fried keyboards with a limited key set, and Jim White programmed around most of the protocol problems they caused.

After seminars and two weeks of becoming familiar with the network, the group split into working groups, each focused on particular sites such as BBN-TENEX, SRI-ARC (NIC), MIT-Multics and MIT-DMCG, and others including UCLA-CCN, HARV-10 and UTAH-10.
sections.eli5: Fourteen students learn the network in a computer classroom, then split into small teams that each study different computers.

sections.title: Early Findings
sections.content:
The group's first comments are listed with the author's remarks in braces. They need more information about access to the NCPs at various sites. They sometimes could not sign in to UCLA-NMC directly from UCSB but could by way of BBN. After running a Fortran or PL-1 program remotely they could only display results, not save them as files.

Other questions were how a user can be sure of being logged out after communications break down, how to contact programmers at other sites, whether there is a best time of day to use each site, and whether sites would also assign a separate identification for test use, as UCLA-NMC did. The group praised the user service at MIT-DMCG and BBN, especially the site survey. The author plans subsequent reports on a periodic basis.
sections.eli5: The students already found problems: some computers were hard to reach, results could not be saved, and it was unclear who to ask for help.
